summary.case_overview: This judgment of a 9-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court of India in Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India addresses whether the right to privacy is a fundamental right under the Constitution of India [Page 1] [Page 15]. The reference arose out of a constitutional challenge to the Government of India's Aadhaar scheme, which collects demographic and biometric data of residents [Page 15]. The Court unanimously held that the right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430] [Page 431]. In doing so, the Court expressly overruled earlier decisions in M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent that they held privacy was not a constitutionally protected right [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430] [Page 431].
summary.facts_of_case: The Government of India propounded the Aadhaar card scheme, under which demographic and biometric data of residents across the country are collected and compiled for various service and subsidy delivery purposes [Page 15]. The scheme was challenged before the Supreme Court on the ground that the collection and compilation of such personal data violates the Right to Privacy [Page 15]. Due to conflicting earlier rulings by larger Benches—specifically an 8-Judge Bench in M.P. Sharma and a 6-Judge Bench in Kharak Singh—the matter was referred to a 9-Judge Constitution Bench to authoritatively determine whether the Right to Privacy is a constitutionally guaranteed fundamental right [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 378]. The 9-Judge Bench was constituted solely to answer this foundational constitutional reference and not to adjudicate the specific statutory validity of the Aadhaar Act on its merits [Page 308] [Page 352].
summary.legal_issues:
1. Whether the Right to Privacy is a fundamental right protected under Part III of the Constitution of India, particularly under Article 21 [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 378] [Page 431].
2. Whether the decision in M.P. Sharma, holding that the Right to Privacy is not protected by the Constitution, lays down the correct legal position [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 378] [Page 430].
3. Whether the majority decision in Kharak Singh, to the extent it held that the Right to Privacy is not a guaranteed fundamental right under the Constitution, reflects the correct legal position [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 15] [Page 430].
summary.important_arguments_or_content: The petitioners, represented by senior counsel including Soli Sorabjee, Gopal Subramanium, Shyam Divan, Arvind Datar, Kapil Sibal, and others, contended that privacy is a primordial, inalienable natural right inherent to human dignity and personal liberty under Article 21 and Part III, and that modern technological advancements enable non-invasive intrusions into personal space without knocking on a citizen's door [Page 378] [Page 405] [Page 428]. The Respondent Union of India, through Attorney General K.K. Venugopal, contended that the Constitution does not expressly guarantee a fundamental right to privacy and that the Constituent Assembly intentionally omitted it [Page 282] [Page 308]. The Attorney General further argued that in a developing nation where millions lack basic necessities like food, shelter, and jobs, the right to life must take primacy over privacy rights [Page 308]. Senior Counsel Rakesh Dwivedi, appearing for the State of Gujarat, urged an intermediate position, submitting that privacy should be evaluated under the US standard of 'reasonable expectation of privacy' and that voluntarily parting with non-sensitive personal information to receive government benefits waives a reasonable expectation of privacy [Page 282].
summary.court_reasoning: The Court reasoned that privacy is an inalienable natural right that inheres in every human being by birth and is not a bounty conferred by the State [Page 4] [Page 8] [Page 9] [Page 15] [Page 19] [Page 36]. M.P. Sharma was overruled because it examined privacy narrowly under Article 20(3) regarding compulsory self-incrimination during search and seizure without adjudicating whether privacy emanated from Article 21 or other Part III guarantees [Page 1] [Page 80] [Page 141] [Page 378]. Kharak Singh was overruled in part because its majority opinion inconsistently invalidated night domiciliary visits while holding that privacy was not a guaranteed fundamental right [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 378]. The Court established that fundamental rights are not water-tight compartments; privacy is an essential condition for individual dignity, autonomy, and the exercise of liberty across Part III rights, including freedom of speech, movement, faith, and personal choices [Page 2] [Page 3] [Page 7] [Page 54] [Page 89] [Page 264] [Page 387]. The Court affirmed that privacy is not absolute and may be restricted by law provided the restriction meets the three-fold test of (i) legality (existence of law), (ii) legitimate state aim, and (iii) proportionality between objects and means [Page 3] [Page 6] [Page 396] [Page 424]. The Court rejected an originalist interpretation, noting the Constitution is a living document that must protect citizens against state and non-state intrusions in a digital age [Page 10] [Page 27] [Page 62] [Page 413] [Page 422]. The Court also affirmed that constitutional rights do not depend on majoritarian acceptance and protect discrete minorities and attributes of identity, including sexual orientation [Page 11] [Page 168] [Page 428] [Page 429], and expressly overruled the majority decision in ADM Jabalpur as an aberration in constitutional jurisprudence [Page 352] [Page 430].
summary.decision_or_conclusion:
The 9-Judge Bench unanimously answered the reference as follows:
(i) The decision in M.P. Sharma holding that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution stands overruled [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430].
(ii) The decision in Kharak Singh to the extent that it holds that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution stands overruled [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430] [Page 431].
(iii) The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 431].
(iv) Decisions subsequent to Kharak Singh enunciating this position lay down the correct position in law [Page 15] [Page 431].
The individual writ petitions were directed to be sent back to the original 3-Judge Bench for adjudication on merits in light of this judgment [Page 5] [Page 352].

summary.simplified_explanation: The Supreme Court of India declared that every individual has a fundamental right to privacy under the Indian Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 431]. The case arose when citizens challenged the Government's Aadhaar program—which collects biometric and personal data—claiming it violated privacy [Page 15]. The Government argued that privacy was not a fundamental right [Page 282] [Page 308]. A 9-judge bench ruled unanimously that privacy is an inherent part of human dignity and personal freedom under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 15] [Page 431]. Older court decisions from 1954 and 1962 that said privacy was not protected were overruled [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430] [Page 431]. The Court clarified that privacy is not absolute; the government can restrict it, but only if there is a valid law, a clear and legitimate goal, and the measure used is proportionate [Page 3] [Page 6] [Page 424].
